## Goal (context only)
STORYFORGE

# STORYFORGE — GAME UI REDESIGN, PHASER INTEGRATION & ASSET ARCHITECTURE

You are a Senior HTML5 Game Engineer, Game UI Designer, Pixel Artist Technical Director, and Frontend Architect.

Your task is to completely redesign the current StoryForge gameplay interface and implement a proper 2D game rendering architecture.

The current implementation is visually unacceptable and must not be incrementally patched.

Build a polished, immersive, playable pixel-art RPG experience.

## 1. Inspect Before Implementing

Inspect the existing repository and identify:
- Current React structure.
- Existing game scene implementation.
- Current game state and interaction logic.
- Existing Go API integration.
- Current contribution submission flow.
- Existing game assets and asset formats.

Preserve working business logic and API contracts.

Do not replace working backend functionality with mock data.

## 2. Technology Stack

Use:
- React + TypeScript + Vite for application UI.
- Phaser 3.90 for 2D game rendering.
- Tailwind CSS for styling.
- shadcn/ui and Radix UI for dialogs, drawers, tabs and popovers.
- Zustand for shared game/UI state.
- Motion for subtle UI transitions.
- Lucide React for icons.

Integration architecture:

- React owns the application interface.
- Phaser owns game world rendering, game objects, animations, camera, scenes and pointer interactions.
- Zustand coordinates shared game and UI state.
- Go Backend remains responsible for APIs, player sessions, Round information and community contributions.

Do not implement game rendering using large collections of HTML div elements.

## 3. Visual Direction

Create a polished, immersive pixel-art RPG experience.

Visual references:
- Modern indie pixel-art adventure games.
- Cozy RPG bedroom environments.
- Point-and-click adventure interfaces.
- Rich environmental details.
- Warm lighting.
- Atmospheric shadows.
- Subtle animated elements.

Avoid:
- Default browser styling.
- Giant gray placeholder rectangles.
- Plain HTML buttons.
- Generic dashboard appearance.
- Unnecessary gradients and excessive glass effects.
- Arbitrary image dimensions.
- Oversized empty whitespace.

The game should look like a real commercial indie RPG.

## 4. Gameplay Layout

Create a full-viewport gameplay layout.

### Desktop

- Game World: approximately 80% width.
- Story Panel: approximately 20% width.
- Header: compact overlay.
- No unnecessary page scrolling.

### Game World

- Full responsive Phaser canvas.
- Correct aspect ratio and scaling.
- Detailed bedroom scene.
- Interactive bookshelf, computer, bed, window and door.
- Hover highlights.
- Object name labels.
- Click-to-interact.
- Character idle animation.
- Character interaction animation.
- Scene transitions.

### Story Panel

- Narrative history.
- Character dialogue.
- Available choices.
- Inventory.
- Current scene title.
- Independent scrolling.

Keep the panel visually integrated with the game rather than looking like a separate website sidebar.

### Mobile

- Game scene remains primary.
- Story and inventory move into a bottom drawer.
- Gameplay controls must remain accessible.

## 5. Game Asset Architecture

This is a critical architectural requirement.

Do not create the entire bedroom as one flattened image.

The game world must be composed of independently managed visual assets so that future AI development cycles can add, replace, animate or modify individual elements without recreating the entire scene.

### 5.1 Layer-based Scene Composition

Organize the bedroom into logical rendering layers:

1. Background:
   - Walls.
   - Floor.
   - Windows and environmental background.
   - Lighting and atmospheric effects.

2. Furniture:
   - Bed.
   - Desk.
   - Bookshelf.
   - Chair.
   - Wardrobe.

3. Interactive Objects:
   - Computer.
   - Books.
   - Door.
   - Window.
   - Personal belongings.

4. Characters:
   - Main boy character.
   - NPCs.
   - Character sprites and animations.

5. Effects:
   - Ambient lighting.
   - Dust particles.
   - Interaction highlights.
   - Visual feedback.
   - Scene transitions.

6. UI Overlay:
   - Object labels.
   - Interaction indicators.
   - Contextual action prompts.

Each layer must have a clear rendering order and independent asset references.

### 5.2 Asset Organization

Create a consistent asset structure:

game/
  public/
    assets/
      worlds/
        the-boys-room/
          backgrounds/
          furniture/
          objects/
          characters/
          effects/
          audio/
      ui/
        icons/
        frames/
        cursors/

  src/
    engine/
    scenes/
    entities/
    systems/
    components/
    assets/
      manifest/
      loaders/
    content/
      worlds/
        the-boys-room/

Create an asset manifest that records:

- Asset ID.
- Asset path.
- Asset type.
- Dimensions.
- Sprite sheet information.
- Animation definitions.
- Origin and anchor points.
- Collision or interaction bounds where applicable.

Use typed TypeScript interfaces for the asset manifest.

### 5.3 Sprite and Animation Requirements

Use individual sprites or sprite sheets where appropriate.

Support:
- Idle animation.
- Walking animation.
- Interaction animation.
- Object state changes.
- NPC animation.
- Animated environmental elements.

Do not stretch small pixel-art sprites.

Use pixel-art-friendly scaling and rendering settings in Phaser.

Preserve consistent pixel density and visual proportions.

### 5.4 Interactive Object Architecture

Every interactive object must be independently configurable.

Example:

{
  "id": "bookshelf",
  "name": "Old Bookshelf",
  "asset": "objects/bookshelf",
  "position": {
    "x": 620,
    "y": 350
  },
  "interaction": {
    "enabled": true,
    "actions": [
      "inspect",
      "push",
      "search"
    ]
  }
}

The example is illustrative. Implement a proper validated schema.

The object system must support:
- Position and scale.
- Rendering layer.
- Interaction bounds.
- Hover state.
- Click event.
- Contextual actions.
- Visibility conditions.
- Persistent state changes.

For example, when the boy opens a secret door behind the bookshelf, the door must remain open when the player returns to the bedroom.

### 5.5 AI-Friendly Asset Architecture

The architecture must support future AI coding cycles.

An AI coding agent should be able to:

- Add a new interactive object.
- Replace a furniture asset.
- Add a character.
- Add character animations.
- Create a new scene.
- Add a new location.
- Modify the bedroom layout.
- Add environmental effects.

These changes should not require rewriting the entire rendering engine.

Separate game runtime logic from game content and asset references.

Do not hardcode every object directly into the Phaser scene implementation.

### 5.6 Asset Quality

Use a consistent pixel-art style across all assets.

If final assets are unavailable:
- Create coherent temporary pixel-art assets.
- Use proper sprites and layered composition.
- Do not use empty gray placeholders.
- Do not use unrelated stock images.
- Document replacement requirements.

Use original or properly licensed assets.

Do not claim that temporary assets are production-ready artwork.

## 6. Opening Scene

World: The Boy's Room.

The boy is sitting in his bedroom.

He looks confused and does not know what to do.

Opening dialogue:

"I don't know what to do next. What should we do?"

Show the first available actions:
- Look around the room.
- Let's explore.

Clicking the bookshelf, computer, bed, window or door should open contextual interactions.

All interactions must update actual game state.

## 7. Header

Display:
- StoryForge logo.
- World name.
- Current Round ID: ROUND-0000001.
- Round status.
- Countdown.
- Sound toggle.
- Settings.

Do not display "Round unavailable" when the API fails without explaining the failure.

Implement proper loading, empty and error states.

## 8. Community Contribution UX

The Suggest What Happens Next action must be accessible without leaving the gameplay screen.

Open a polished modal or side drawer.

Include:
- Prompt textarea.
- Remaining contribution count.
- Submission button.
- Submission success/error feedback.
- Community contribution history.

Connect to the existing Go backend.

Do not use Firebase.
Do not introduce a database.
Do not put Git credentials in the browser.

## 9. Engineering Requirements

- Proper Phaser lifecycle and cleanup in React.
- Prevent duplicate Phaser game instances.
- Handle browser resizing.
- Handle device pixel ratio.
- Keep game state synchronized with React.
- Avoid duplicated state ownership.
- Implement typed event interfaces between Phaser and React.
- Ensure interactive objects are keyboard-accessible where appropriate.
- Handle missing game assets gracefully.
- Implement asset loading and validation.
- Keep scene definitions separate from rendering logic.
- Ensure asset manifest references are validated.
- Support persistent object states.
- Avoid unnecessary asset loading and memory leaks.

## 10. Acceptance Criteria

The redesign is complete only when:

1. The game occupies approximately 80% of the desktop viewport.
2. The story panel occupies approximately 20%.
3. No giant gray placeholders remain.
4. The bedroom fills the available game viewport correctly.
5. The bedroom uses independently managed visual layers.
6. Furniture and interactive objects are separate assets.
7. The character has working animations.
8. Objects can be clicked.
9. Hover states identify interactive objects.
10. Object interaction changes actual game state.
11. Dialogue and choices update correctly.
12. Inventory updates correctly.
13. Persistent object states work.
14. Community contribution modal works.
15. Submission uses the real backend.
16. Round status is retrieved from the real API.
17. Mobile layout works.
18. No horizontal overflow or unintended page scrolling exists.
19. Phaser instances are properly cleaned up.
20. Future AI development can add assets and objects without rewriting the game engine.

Run the application, inspect the actual browser rendering, and fix visual issues before declaring completion.

Do not consider a successful TypeScript build sufficient.

The actual UI and gameplay must be visually inspected at desktop and mobile resolutions.

## 11. Implementation Strategy

Implement in this order:

Phase A:
- Inspect the current application.
- Establish the visual design system.
- Implement the new responsive application shell.

Phase B:
- Integrate Phaser.
- Implement scene rendering.
- Implement layer-based asset architecture.
- Implement the initial bedroom.

Phase C:
- Implement characters and animations.
- Implement interactive objects.
- Implement contextual actions.
- Implement dialogue and choices.
- Implement inventory and persistent game state.

Phase D:
- Integrate the Story Panel.
- Integrate Round status.
- Integrate Community Contribution.
- Connect the existing Go backend.

Phase E:
- Test desktop and mobile.
- Test Phaser lifecycle.
- Test asset loading.
- Test interaction and state persistence.
- Fix all visual and functional defects.

Do not stop after producing a plan or documentation.

Implement the actual working application and verify it in the browser.
